questions.q: Explain in your own words how the author uses the monsoon season to create atmosphere in the first half of the chapter. Why is monsoon not just a weather description here?
questions.a: The monsoon acts as an emotional catalyst — its arrival triggers the sensory flood (sound of rain on pond, smell of wet earth, frogs' chorus) that unlocks the narrator's buried memories. It is not mere weather because it mirrors the narrator's internal state: overwhelming, cleansing, and cyclical like memory itself. A wrong answer describing monsoon as "rainy season background" misses its function as a memory-trigger and mood-setter.

questions.q: Write a 50-word sensory paragraph describing a place from your childhood that no longer exists, using at least three techniques from this chapter (onomatopoeia, tactile imagery, olfactory trigger, cyclical time marker).
questions.a: A strong answer will include: (1) a sound-word like "tapatap" or "jharjhar", (2) a touch memory like "mitti ki saundhi mehak haathon par", (3) a smell that transports — "pehli baarish ki khushboo", (4) a time loop — "har saawan wapas le aata hai". A weak answer lists facts ("my grandmother's house had a neem tree") without sensory immersion or emotional resonance.
